*By the end of this note, the student will be able to distinguish, investigate, and clinically manage bacterial meningitis and encephalitis in a Kenyan ward setting; verify all drug choices and regimens against the Kenya MoH guidelines and local hospital formularies.*

Encephalitis: Acute inflammation of the brain parenchyma itself, distinguished clinically from meningitis by early alteration in brain function (confusion, behavioral changes, focal neurological deficits, or seizures).
| Viral meningitis/encephalitis | Prodromal viral illness, less severe CSF changes | Viral PCR in CSF, absence of fungal/parasitic organisms |

qs.q: What is the expected rate of progression to coma and death in children with herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) encephalitis if antiviral therapy is not administered?
qs.e: HSV-1 is a major cause of severe sporadic encephalitis that leads to coma and death in 70% of cases without antiviral treatment. Lower figures underestimate the mortality associated with untreated HSV-1 infection.

qs.q: Post-mortem histopathological examination of brain tissue from a child who died of viral encephalitis reveals lesions concentrated predominantly in the basal structures. Which pathogen is most characteristically associated with this anatomical predilection?
qs.e: Rabies virus has a specific predilection for infecting and destroying basal structures of the brain. In contrast, HSV-1 classically targets the temporal cerebral cortex, and arboviruses generally affect the entire brain.

qs.q: Which pathogen is an important cause of severe, sporadic encephalitis in children and adults, progressing to coma and death in 70% of cases if untreated?
qs.e: Herpes simplex virus type 1 is a major cause of severe, sporadic encephalitis that can progress to high mortality without antiviral therapy. HSV type 2 causes severe diffuse brain involvement primarily in neonates via vertical transmission.

qs.q: In cases of Herpes simplex virus encephalitis, which region of the brain is classically and severely affected?
qs.e: In HSV encephalitis, the cerebral cortex, classically the temporal lobes in HSV-1 encephalitis, is often severely affected. Conversely, rabies has a predilection for the basal structures.

qs.q: A patient with suspected HSV encephalitis is evaluated in the emergency department. What is the most appropriate management regarding antiviral therapy?
o: Start intravenous aciclovir immediately without waiting for PCR results
Wait for confirmatory lumbar puncture results before initiating therapy
Administer oral oseltamivir within forty-eight hours of symptom onset
Prescribe topical clotrimazole to prevent secondary mucosal lesions
qs.e: HSV encephalitis is a medical emergency requiring immediate IV aciclovir therapy rather than delaying for diagnostic test results. Waiting for PCR results significantly worsens neurological outcomes.
qs.s: Antifungals, Antivirals, Antihelminthics & Antiprotozoals — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A child being treated for acute chickenpox is given salicylates to control fever and subsequently develops fulminant encephalitis and severe hepatic dysfunction. What syndrome is strongly associated with this medication use during VZV infection?
qs.e: Fulminant encephalitis during chickenpox can be part of Reye's syndrome if salicylates are administered to children. Post-herpetic neuralgia is a complication of shingles involving chronic pain rather than salicylate-induced liver and brain dysfunction.
qs.s: Herpesviruses: HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Tx — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: In a patient presenting with an infectious encephalitis, resident microglia form small aggregates around small foci of tissue necrosis and actively engulf dying neurons. What is the term for this latter process?
qs.e: Neuronophagia describes microglia and macrophages congregating around and engulfing dying neurons during CNS infections or severe injury. Chromatolysis instead describes the reactive morphological changes seen in the neuronal cell body during axonal repair.
qs.s: Neuropathology: CNS Neuronal & Astrocyte Injury Reactions — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A medical officer suspects viral encephalitis in a patient presenting with acute fever and altered mental status. Which diagnostic modality offers the highest sensitivity and specificity for detecting viral nucleic acid directly from cerebrospinal fluid?
o: Viral cell culture with cytopathic effect
qs.e: Molecular PCR tests detect viral nucleic acid directly and are the gold standard for diagnosing viral infections in CSF due to their high sensitivity and specificity. Serology and culture are generally slower or used for past exposure or isolation.
qs.s: Medical Virology Semester 3 Crash Revision — Notes: MCQs

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Encephalitis is inflammation of brain parenchyma causing altered mental status, seizures, and focal deficits. Prompt recognition, investigation and treatment of the underlying cause are essential to reduce mortality and long‑term disability.

sections.p: Encephalitis is brain parenchymal inflammation confirmed by clinical features plus supportive CSF, imaging or histology. Diagnosis requires exclusion of mimics.
b: Fever, new onset altered consciousness, seizures, focal neurologic signs
CSF: pleocytosis (>5 cells/µL), elevated protein, normal/low glucose
MRI: T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in gray matter, especially temporal lobes

t.b: Does the CSF show inflammatory changes? → Pleocytosis and protein rise support encephalitis; normal CSF suggests alternative diagnosis.
Is there focal parenchymal inflammation? → Hyperintense lesions confirm involvement; normal MRI early does not exclude disease.
Which infectious agent is present? → Positive result directs targeted therapy; negative does not rule out infection.

sections.p: Severity is graded by level of consciousness, need for intensive care, and presence of complications.
b: Mild: alert, no ICU, no seizures
Moderate: confusion, seizures controlled with medication
Severe: coma, refractory seizures, respiratory failure

sections.p: Identify the aetiology to guide therapy; infections dominate, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Viral: HSV‑1 (most common worldwide), Japanese encephalitis, dengue, Zika, rabies
Bacterial: Listeria, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (TB meningitis with encephalitic features)
Parasitic: Plasmodium falciparum (cerebral malaria)
Autoimmune: NMDA‑receptor encephalitis, post‑infectious ADEM

sections.p: Clinical picture evolves over hours to days, often after a prodrome of fever or viral illness.
b: Fever, headache, neck stiffness
Altered mental status ranging from lethargy to coma
New seizures or focal neurologic deficits
Behavioral changes, hallucinations in autoimmune forms

sections.p: Targeted tests answer key clinical questions while considering resource limits.

t.b: Is HSV likely? → Positive directs acyclovir; if unavailable, start empiric therapy.
Is cerebral malaria present? → Positive leads to antimalarial treatment; if unavailable, treat empirically in endemic area.
Are seizures ongoing or subclinical? → Diffuse slowing supports encephalitis; periodic discharges suggest specific viral causes.

sections.p: Recognise features that predict rapid deterioration.
b: Rapid progression to coma
Refractory seizures or status epilepticus
Brain herniation signs (pupillary changes)
Multiorgan failure

sections.p: Treat the cause first, then provide supportive care and monitor for complications.
b: Empiric IV acyclovir for suspected HSV until PCR negative
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics if bacterial meningitis cannot be excluded
Antimalarial (artesunate) in endemic regions with compatible presentation
High‑dose steroids for autoimmune encephalitis after infectious work‑up
Seizure control with benzodiazepines then levetiracetam; avoid phenytoin in hepatic failure

sections.p: After acute care, assess neurologic recovery and vaccinate where appropriate.
b: Neurorehabilitation for persistent deficits
Vaccination: Japanese encephalitis, measles, varicella, rabies post‑exposure prophylaxis
Education on mosquito bite avoidance in endemic areas

sections.p: Conditions that mimic encephalitis must be ruled out.
b: Meningitis (meningeal signs predominate)
Stroke or intracranial hemorrhage
Severe metabolic encephalopathy (hypoglycaemia, hepatic failure)
Psychiatric disorders or conversion

sections.p: Beware of false‑negative or misleading findings.
b: Early MRI may be normal despite encephalitis
CSF PCR can be negative in HSV if performed after 10 days
Peripheral eosinophilia may suggest parasitic infection but can be absent

whenToSeekHelp: New onset seizures or status epilepticus
Signs of brain herniation (unequal pupils, abnormal breathing)

faq.q: Why start acyclovir before a definitive HSV diagnosis?
faq.a: HSV encephalitis has high mortality; early therapy dramatically improves outcome, and delay waiting for PCR is unsafe.

faq.q: Can encephalitis be viral without fever?
faq.a: Yes; some viral encephalitides (e.g., HSV) may present with minimal fever, especially in immunocompromised patients.
After infectious causes are excluded, steroids are used for autoimmune encephalitis or to reduce cerebral edema in severe cases.
